summary: This standards-track RFC describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP headers. It obsoletes RFC 6145.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says how a translator turns an IPv4 packet into an IPv6 packet and back again. The translator swaps the header, rewrites the addresses using a fixed rule, converts the error messages that the two versions of ICMP use, and fixes up the checksum that covers the header. It also explains what happens when the packet is too big for the link on the other side.

questions: how does ipv4 to ipv6 translation work
what is the difference between stateless and stateful translation
how are icmp messages translated between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: How a translator converts IPv4 packets into IPv6 packets and back, header by header.

tldr.problem: Hosts on an IPv4 network and hosts on an IPv6 network cannot talk directly. A translator between the two domains has to convert each packet's header, and the two header formats differ in size, in how they report errors and in how they handle fragmentation.
tldr.mechanism: The translator replaces the IPv4 header with an IPv6 header, or the reverse, and leaves the data untouched. It maps addresses with a stateless algorithm, translates ICMP types and codes between the two versions, and adjusts the transport checksum because it covers the IP header.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 6145, deprecated the algorithm that generates IPv6 atomic fragments, and moved the discussion of address mapping algorithms into one section. The translator must support the stateless mapping of RFC 6052.

today: RFC 7915 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 6145. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The IPv4/IPv6 Translation Model
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 6145. It gives the algorithm an IP/ICMP translator follows to convert an IPv4 packet into an IPv6 packet and back.

The translation model consists of two or more network domains connected by one or more translators. Readers are expected to have read the framework of RFC 6144, and an implementation must support one or more of the address mapping algorithms defined in Section 6.

The translating function does not translate any IPv4 options, and it does not translate IPv6 extension headers except the Fragment Header. The issues and algorithms in translating datagrams that carry TCP segments are described in RFC 5382. Fragmented IPv4 UDP packets that do not contain a UDP checksum are not of significant use on the Internet and will generally not be translated, although a translator configured to forward packets without a UDP checksum will translate them. Fragmented ICMP and ICMPv6 packets will not be translated at all.

The header translation is consistent with the requirements of multicast IP and ICMP headers, but IPv4 multicast addresses cannot be mapped to IPv6 multicast addresses using the unicast mapping rule of RFC 6052.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator sits between an IPv4 network and an IPv6 network and rewrites each packet as it passes. This document is the rulebook for that rewriting. It does not cover IPv4 options, most IPv6 extension headers, or TCP-specific problems.

sections.title: Stateless and Stateful Modes
sections.content:
An IP/ICMP translator has two modes of operation, stateless and stateful. In both cases the document assumes a system with an IPv4 address but no IPv6 address is communicating with a system that has an IPv6 address but no IPv4 address, or that the two do not have contiguous routing connectivity, or that they have contiguous routing connectivity but are interacting through masking addresses, that is, hairpinning, and are therefore forced to have their communications translated.

In stateless mode the translator converts IPv4 addresses to IPv6 and back solely from its own configuration and from information inside the packet being translated. For the default behaviour of RFC 6052, a specific IPv6 address range represents IPv4 systems, and the IPv6 systems have addresses that can be mapped algorithmically to a subset of the service provider's IPv4 addresses. The stateless translator keeps no dynamic session or binding state, so there is no requirement that the packets of a single session or flow traverse a single translator.

In stateful mode a specific IPv6 address range, made of IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses, typically represents IPv4 systems, and the IPv6 nodes may use any other IPv6 addresses. The translator continuously maintains a dynamic translation table of bindings between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and likely also the Layer-4 identifiers, used in the translated packets. The translation of a given packet therefore depends on how earlier packets of the same session or flow were translated, so stateful translation generally requires all packets of a single flow to traverse the same translator.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateless translator rewrites addresses with a fixed formula and remembers nothing between packets, so any translator on the path can handle any packet. A stateful translator keeps a table of which address belongs to which session, so all the packets of one session have to go through the same translator.

sections.title: Translating from IPv4 to IPv6
sections.content:
When the translator receives an IPv4 datagram addressed towards the IPv6 domain, it replaces the IPv4 header with an IPv6 header and updates the transport checksum as needed, if that transport is supported. The data portion of the packet is left unchanged, and the packet is then forwarded based on the IPv6 destination address.

Path MTU discovery is mandatory in IPv6 and optional in IPv4, and the header sizes differ: 20 or more octets for IPv4 and 40 octets for IPv6. The translator must behave as a router, so it must send a Packet Too Big error message or fragment the packet when the packet size exceeds the MTU of the next-hop interface.

When the IPv4 node performs path MTU discovery by setting the Don't Fragment (DF) bit, path MTU discovery can operate end to end across the translator, and an IPv6 Fragment Header is only included if the IPv4 packet is already fragmented. When the IPv4 sender does not set the DF bit, the translator must ensure the packet does not exceed the path MTU on the IPv6 side, by fragmenting it with Fragment Headers so that it fits in 1280-byte IPv6 packets, the minimum IPv6 MTU. The translator must provide a configuration function so the administrator can raise that threshold when the real minimum IPv6 MTU of the network is larger, which reduces the chance of adding a Fragment Header. When the DF bit is not set, the translator must not include a Fragment Header for the non-fragmented IPv6 packets.

IPv4 options are ignored and the packet translated normally, except that an unexpired source route option makes the translator discard the packet and return an ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable, Source Route Failed error, Type 3 Code 5.

The translator should make sure that packets belonging to the same flow leave it in the order in which they arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: Going from IPv4 to IPv6, the translator replaces the header, keeps the data as it is, and forwards on the new address. If the packet is too big for the IPv6 link, it splits it into fragments, because IPv6 routers never split a packet themselves.

sections.title: Setting the IPv6 Header Fields
sections.content:
The IPv6 header fields are set as follows. The version is 6. The traffic class is by default copied from the IPv4 Type Of Service octet, and an implementation should offer a configurable option to ignore the IPv4 TOS and always set the traffic class to zero. The flow label is zero. The payload length is the total length value from the IPv4 header minus the size of the IPv4 header and any IPv4 options. The next header is ICMPv6, value 58, for ICMPv4 value 1, and otherwise the protocol field copied from the IPv4 header. The hop limit is derived from the IPv4 TTL; since the translator is a router it must decrement one of them and must check for zero and send the ICMPv4 TTL Exceeded or ICMPv6 Hop Limit Exceeded error.

The source and destination addresses are mapped using the algorithms of Section 6. If the translator gets an illegal source address such as 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1, it should silently discard the packet, except when translating ICMPv4 error messages, where the illegal source address is translated for the purpose of troubleshooting.

When a Fragment Header has to be added, the payload length is the IPv4 total length plus 8 for the Fragment Header, minus the IPv4 header and options, and the next header is the Fragment Header, value 44. In the Fragment Header the next header follows the same rule, the fragment offset is copied from the IPv4 header, the More Fragments flag is copied, and the identification field takes the low-order 16 bits of the IPv4 Identification field with the high-order 16 bits set to zero, so that the fragments are correctly reassembled.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the new header is copied or calculated: the length shrinks by the size of the old header, the hop limit comes from the old TTL, and the addresses are rewritten. The flow label is always zero, and the traffic class usually copies the old type of service byte.

sections.title: Translating ICMPv4 into ICMPv6
sections.content:
All ICMPv4 messages that are translated need the ICMPv6 checksum calculated as part of the translation, because ICMPv6, unlike ICMPv4, has a pseudo-header checksum like UDP and TCP. All ICMPv4 packets must have their Type translated, and ICMPv4 error messages must also have the included IP header translated.

Among the query messages, Echo and Echo Reply, types 8 and 0, become types 128 and 129, with the checksum adjusted for the type change and for the pseudo-header. Information Request and Reply, types 15 and 16, Timestamp and Timestamp Reply, types 13 and 14, and Address Mask Request and Reply, types 17 and 18, are all obsoleted in ICMPv6 and are silently dropped. Router Advertisement, type 9, and Router Solicitation, type 10, are single-hop messages and are silently dropped, as are unknown ICMPv4 types and the normal IGMP messages.

Among the error messages, Destination Unreachable, type 3, becomes type 1 with the code translated. Codes 0 and 1, net and host unreachable, become code 0, no route to destination. Code 2, protocol unreachable, becomes an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem, type 4 code 1, with the pointer at the IPv6 Next Header field. Code 3, port unreachable, becomes code 4. Code 4, fragmentation needed with DF set, becomes an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, type 2, with code 0; the MTU field is adjusted for the difference between the header sizes but never set below the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 bytes. Codes 5, 6, 7, 8, 11 and 12 become code 0; codes 9, 10, 13 and 15 become code 1; and code 14 is silently dropped, as are all other code values.

Redirect, type 5, and Alternative Host Address, type 6, are single-hop or obsolete and are silently dropped, as is Source Quench, type 4. Time Exceeded, type 11, becomes type 3 with the code unchanged. Parameter Problem, type 12, becomes type 4; code 0 and code 2 become code 0 with the pointer updated, and code 1 and all other codes are silently dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The two versions of ICMP use different numbers for the same message, so the translator renumbers them. Some ICMPv4 messages have no ICMPv6 equivalent and are thrown away without a reply. The checksum is recomputed because ICMPv6 checksums cover the IP header as well.

sections.title: Translating from IPv6 to IPv4
sections.content:
When the translator receives an IPv6 datagram addressed towards the IPv4 domain, it replaces the IPv6 header with an IPv4 header, leaves the data portion unchanged, and forwards based on the IPv4 destination address. Because the ICMPv6, TCP, UDP and DCCP headers contain checksums that cover the IP header, if the address mapping algorithm is not checksum neutral the checksum must be evaluated before translation and the ICMP and transport-layer headers must be updated.

If there is no IPv6 Fragment Header, the version is 4, the Internet Header Length is 5 because there are no IPv4 options, and the Type of Service octet is by default copied from the IPv6 traffic class. The total length is the IPv6 payload length plus the size of the IPv4 header. The identification field is set by a fragment identification generator at the translator. The More Fragments flag is zero, and the Don't Fragment flag is zero when the translated IPv4 packet is 1260 bytes or smaller and one otherwise. The fragment offset is all zeros. The time to live is derived from the IPv6 hop limit and decremented as at any router.

An IPv6 link must have an MTU of 1280 bytes or greater, and the corresponding limit for IPv4 is 68 bytes. The difference is accommodated in two ways. When an ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed packet is translated, the MTU in the resulting ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is never set below 1280, so IPv6 nodes never meet a path MTU below the minimum IPv6 link MTU. And when the resulting IPv4 packet is 1260 bytes or smaller the translator sends it with the Don't Fragment bit cleared, and otherwise with the bit set. Path MTU discovery then works end to end for paths whose MTU is not smaller than 1280, which corresponds to 1260 in the IPv4 domain; on paths with IPv4 links below 1260 the IPv4 routers fragment the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Going the other way, the translator swaps the IPv6 header for an IPv4 one and recalculates the transport checksum, because the checksum covers the header that just changed. A packet that fits within 1260 bytes is sent with the do-not-fragment bit clear so that IPv4 routers can still split it if they must.

sections.title: Mapping of IP Addresses
sections.content:
The translator must support the stateless address mapping algorithm of RFC 6052, which is the default behaviour. The stateless translator should support the explicit address mapping algorithm of RFC 7757, and should support RFC 6791 for handling ICMP and ICMPv6 packets.

Implementations may support both the stateless and the stateful translation modes, for example NAT64 as described in RFC 6146. They may also support the stateless NAT64 function, for example MAP-T Customer Edge or MAP-T Border Relay in RFC 7599.
sections.plainLanguage: The addresses on each side are rewritten with a fixed rule so that the same IPv4 address always becomes the same IPv6 address and the other way round. That rule is defined in RFC 6052, and translators must support it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using stateless IP/ICMP translators does not introduce any new security issues beyond those already present in IPv4 and IPv6 and in the routing protocols used to make packets reach the translator.

There are potential issues in deriving an IPv4 address from an IPv6 address, particularly for addresses such as broadcast or loopback addresses and the non-IPv4-translatable IPv6 addresses. RFC 6052 addresses these issues.

The IPsec Authentication Header cannot be used for NAT44 or NAT64. As with IPv4-to-IPv4 network address translation, packets with tunnel mode Encapsulating Security Payload can be translated, since tunnel mode ESP does not depend on header fields before the ESP header. Transport mode ESP fails with IPv6-to-IPv4 translation unless checksum-neutral addresses are used. In both cases the IPsec ESP endpoints will normally detect the presence of the translator and encapsulate ESP in UDP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator adds no new security problems of its own, but it does break some forms of IPsec. Tunnelled IPsec still works, because the translator does not touch the part of the packet it protects.

viz.caption: HOW EACH IPv6 HEADER FIELD IS FILLED IN

cells: Copied from the IPv4 Type Of Service octet by default
IPv4 total length, minus the IPv4 header and any options
58 for ICMPv4, otherwise the IPv4 protocol field
Mapped with the algorithm of Section 6

items.label: Destination Unreachable
items.desc: Stays type 1, with the code translated.

items.label: Packet Too Big
items.desc: Produced from ICMPv4 code 4, with the MTU never below 1280.

items.label: Time Exceeded
items.desc: Comes from ICMPv4 type 11, code unchanged.

items.label: Parameter Problem
items.desc: Comes from ICMPv4 type 12, with the pointer updated.

left.title: IPv4 to IPv6
left.desc: The IPv4 header is replaced with an IPv6 header and the addresses are mapped. The data is unchanged.

right.title: IPv6 to IPv4
right.desc: The IPv6 header is replaced with an IPv4 header, the addresses are mapped, and the transport checksum is recalculated.
